steps.en: Pulsed wave Doppler samples velocity at one chosen depth and nowhere else. The probe emits a pulse, waits for the echo from the sample volume, and the returning frequency shift gives the velocity at that exact spot. The price of this range gating is a speed limit: the Nyquist limit, half the pulse repetition frequency. Flow faster than the limit wraps around the baseline as aliasing. Mastering pulsed wave means placing a small sample volume exactly on the flow you want, keeping the beam parallel to it, and recognising aliasing as physics rather than disease.
Find the flow on colour first, then drop the sample volume gate exactly on the jet or orifice of interest.
Place the gate at the mitral leaflet tips for inflow, or just below the aortic cusps for outflow velocity.
Steer the beam as parallel to flow as possible and keep the angle under 20 degrees.
Set a small gate of a few millimetres so neighbouring flows do not contaminate the trace.
Scale the velocity range so the envelope fills two thirds of the display without wrapping.
Turn the wall filter low for venous and inflow signals and higher only to clear wall thump from fast jets.
Sample volume sitting off the true flow core. Fix: Reposition the gate step by step along the jet. A gate upstream records slower flow and a gate inside the orifice records noise.
Beam to flow angle above 20 degrees. Fix: Realign the window or accept and document the angle. Cosine error only ever underreads velocity.
Reading an aliased peak as the real velocity. Fix: Raise the scale, shift the baseline, or move to continuous wave. Never report a wrapped peak as the true velocity.
Faint trace from a tiny gate with high gain. Fix: Enlarge the gate slightly and lower the gain until the envelope is dense but the background is clean.
Nyquist limit. Half the pulse repetition frequency; flow above it aliases. Source: ASE 2019 transthoracic examination, section on spectral Doppler optimisation
Reliable pulsed wave velocity range. Faithful below about 1.5 to 2 m per s; use continuous wave above this. Source: ASE 2019 transthoracic examination, section on pulsed wave Doppler and aliasing
Angle error. Keep the beam to flow angle under 20 degrees; error grows with the cosine of the angle. Source: ASE 2019 transthoracic examination, section on Doppler alignment
Mitral inflow recording site. Sample volume at the leaflet tips in the apical four chamber. Source: ASE 2019 transthoracic examination, section on mitral inflow Doppler
High pulse repetition frequency extends the range but invites range ambiguity from a second gate, so check what you are hearing.
Annular tissue velocities need tissue Doppler presets, not blood flow settings, or the wall filter wipes them out.
Atrial fibrillation varies every beat, so average several envelopes rather than tracing one tall one.

q.en: What does the pulsed wave sample volume give you?

o.en: It samples all depths at once
It samples velocity at one chosen depth only

why.en: Range gating returns velocity from the gate position alone, which is why gate placement decides the result.

o.en: Equal to the pulse repetition frequency

why.en: The sampling limit is half the pulse repetition frequency. Shifts above it wrap around as aliasing.

q.en: The aortic jet wraps over the baseline on pulsed wave. What do you do?

o.en: Raise the wall filter to maximum
Raise the scale, shift the baseline, or switch to continuous wave
Report the wrapped peak as measured

why.en: Aliasing means the velocity exceeds the Nyquist limit, so rescale, shift the baseline, or move to continuous wave for the peak.

q.en: What beam to flow angle keeps cosine error small?

why.en: Below 20 degrees the cosine error stays small. Larger angles underread velocity, and no correction is trusted above 20 degrees.
